title: Airframe
object: Airframe structure of a four-seat high-wing strut-braced light aircraft: the wing's spars, ribs and skin, the strut and its fittings, the semi-monocoque fuselage's frames, longerons, stringers, firewall and door frame, and the tailplane and fin
idea: A strut turns a long cantilever into a short propped beam: the wing's bending moment, and the spar it needs, fall to a fifth
summary: The lift, n·W shared by two wings, is spread along the span (Schrenk). Each wing is a beam pinned at the cabin roof and propped by the strut at WS 3000; statics gives the strut's reaction, and since the strut is a two-force member its tension follows from its 25.6° angle: 9.8 kN at 1 g, 37 kN at the 3.8 g limit. The spar's bending moment peaks over the strut at 8.4 kN·m at 3.8 g, against 39 kN·m at the root of the same wing without a strut. In the front spar's caps σ = M/(h·A) reaches 200 MPa at limit with the strut's push, below 2024-T3's yield, and 1.5 times that stays below its ultimate (reserve factor 1.42); unbraced it would be 713 MPa. A 50 ft/s gust at V_C gives 3.75 g, just inside the manoeuvre limit.
usedFor: Aircraft structures courses: lift distribution, shear and bending-moment diagrams, a statically determinate braced beam, spar-cap stress and reserve factors
Pilot and engineer training: what the load factor does to the wing, why there is a limit load and an ultimate factor, gust loads at V_C
Reading an airframe drawing: semi-monocoque frames, longerons and stringers, spar sections, fittings in double shear
